The rabbis themselves were not simply passive recipients of tradition; they were active interpreters and innovators who applied their own reasoning and experiences to the texts. Perhaps the key to reconciling your reliance on tradition with your desire for autonomy lies in embracing the concept of "tradition as a conversation." Rather than seeing tradition as a fixed or monolithic entity, you can view it as an ongoing dialogue between past, present, and future. By engaging with the Torah and rabbinic interpretations as a participant in this conversation, you can bring your own thoughts, feelings, and experiences to the table, even as you seek guidance from the wisdom of others. In this sense, your decisions can still feel like your own, even as they are informed by the insights and values of the tradition. Ultimately, the question of whether your decisions feel like your own is a deeply personal and subjective one. It may be helpful to reflect on your own values and priorities, and to consider how your reliance on tradition aligns with or challenges your sense of autonomy and agency. The whole family is involved in this because that’s just the way my family is and everyone expects me to help out my cousin with his current custody situation to get him more time with his son. WIBTA for telling him I will not allow his son to sleep in our house and completely jeopardizing his court case?
